drills.q: Explain why GCP VPCs being global changes multi-region design compared to AWS, with a concrete example.
drills.a: A GCP VPC spans every region as one resource; subnets are regional but reachability between them is automatic over Google's backbone -- no peering, no Transit Gateway. Example: a prod-vpc with subnet prod-us (us-central1) and subnet prod-eu (europe-west1) can reach each other the moment both subnets exist, with only firewall rules able to block traffic. On AWS, the same topology needs either VPC peering between two regional VPCs or a Transit Gateway with route table propagation configured explicitly per region -- reachability is opt-in, not default.

drills.q: A firewall rule meant only for bastion hosts in one region is unexpectedly allowing SSH from instances in another region. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: GCP firewall rules are VPC-scoped (global) by default -- without an explicit target (tags or service accounts), a rule applies to every matching instance in every region of that VPC. There's no native region-scope field on a firewall rule. Fix: add a target tag or target service account matching only the intended bastion instances; region-level restriction has to be achieved through instance targeting, not a rule-level region filter.

drills.q: Design the Shared VPC + IAM structure for a platform team supporting three product teams that must not reach each other's subnets.
drills.a: One host project (platform team owned) with one subnet per product team. Each team's principals get roles/compute.networkUser scoped to their own subnet only (via IAM conditions or subnet-level bindings), never project-wide on the host. Because the VPC is global-scoped by default for firewall rules, isolation between teams' subnets must be enforced explicitly via deny-by-default firewall rules scoped with target tags/service accounts per team -- Shared VPC's IAM layer controls who can deploy where, not network-level traffic isolation, which is a separate firewall-rule design problem.

drills.q: Compare how GCP's global external Application Load Balancer achieves geo-routing and failover to how AWS achieves the same outcome.
drills.a: GCP: one global anycast IP announced from every Google PoP; traffic enters at the nearest PoP and rides the private backbone to the nearest healthy backend -- this is the load balancer's native architecture, with failover driven by health checks and no DNS dependency. AWS: ALB/NLB are always regional, so equivalent behavior requires layering Route 53 latency/geo routing (DNS-based, subject to TTL/caching delay) with AWS Global Accelerator (a separate anycast-IP service) in front of per-region ALBs -- multiple services combined rather than one integrated resource.

drills.q: Why do static per-IP rate limits in Cloud Armor fail against a distributed botnet attack, and what's the correct mitigation layer?
drills.a: A botnet spreads requests across thousands of rotating source IPs, so no individual IP's request volume crosses a per-IP threshold even though aggregate load on the backend is severe -- each attacking IP looks like normal traffic in isolation. The correct mitigation is Adaptive Protection (Cloud Armor Enterprise tier), which uses ML-based anomaly detection against the backend's own aggregate traffic baseline rather than relying on any single per-IP dimension. Simply lowering the per-IP threshold trades this failure for a different one: blocking legitimate users behind shared NAT/CGNAT whose aggregate traffic now exceeds the lowered bar.

drills.q: Explain Private Service Connect's producer/consumer model and why it avoids the IP-overlap coordination problem VPC peering has.
drills.a: A producer publishes a service attachment; a consumer creates a PSC endpoint (a forwarding rule) in their own subnet pointing at that attachment, getting a private IP inside their own VPC with no peering connection formed between the two networks. Because there's no peering, the producer's and consumer's VPCs never need non-overlapping IP ranges relative to each other -- VPC peering, by contrast, requires the two peered networks' CIDR ranges not to overlap anywhere, which becomes a real coordination burden at scale across many teams/orgs. PSC also lets the producer control exactly which consumers connect via accept lists, rather than exposing the whole peered network's routes.

drills.q: When is Dedicated Interconnect the wrong choice for a mid-size enterprise's hybrid connectivity, and what should they use instead?
drills.a: Dedicated Interconnect requires a 10Gbps or 100Gbps port commitment plus the customer's own colocation facility presence -- a large fixed cost relative to what many mid-size workloads sustain. Partner Interconnect, routed through a supported service provider, offers VLAN attachments from 50Mbps up with no colocation requirement, lower entry cost, and faster provisioning. Dedicated's economics only win once sustained bandwidth utilization is high enough that its lower per-GiB egress rate and lack of provider fees offset the higher fixed port cost -- validate against actual traffic volume, not assumed future growth, before committing.

drills.q: A candidate claims 'Cloud Armor is basically AWS WAF, just renamed.' What's the precise correction?
drills.a: Functionally comparable: both give L7 WAF rules, rate limiting, and bot/DDoS mitigation attached to a load balancer. The gap: Cloud Armor sits in front of GCP's global anycast load balancer, so volumetric attacks are structurally absorbed and distributed across Google's entire edge network before Cloud Armor's rules even fire. AWS WAF on a bare regional ALB doesn't get that same dilution unless separately paired with CloudFront or Global Accelerator, which are globally distributed edge networks in their own right -- the fair comparison is Cloud Armor+global-LB vs AWS-WAF+CloudFront, not vs a bare regional ALB deployment.

drills.q: Walk through what operationally changes when migrating a two-region AWS Transit-Gateway-based topology to GCP.
drills.a: Transit Gateway's centralized routing (route tables, attachments, propagation rules per VPC) mostly disappears -- if both regions' resources belong to the same org/environment, they become subnets of one GCP VPC with reachability by default. What replaces Transit Gateway's routing control is disciplined firewall-rule scoping (since the GCP default is permissive-within-VPC rather than requiring explicit route propagation) and, for team isolation, Shared VPC with per-subnet IAM grants instead of separate VPCs stitched by TGW attachments. The security model inverts: AWS defaults to explicit reachability with implicit isolation; GCP defaults to implicit reachability with explicit isolation -- a team that doesn't internalize this can end up with a flatter, more permissive network than intended.

drills.q: A workload needs to consume a SaaS vendor's API privately without touching the public internet, and the vendor also runs on GCP. Design the connectivity, and state what would make it impossible.
drills.a: If the vendor publishes a PSC service attachment, create a PSC endpoint in the consumer's own VPC subnet pointing at it -- private IP, no internet transit, no IP-overlap coordination, vendor controls access via their accept list. It becomes impossible (or requires a fallback) if the vendor doesn't support PSC publishing at all (only offers public API endpoints or VPN-based access) -- fallback options are Cloud VPN/Interconnect plus vendor-side IP allowlisting, or accepting public-internet-with-TLS access as the only vendor-supported option.

drills.q: Why does global-VPC reachability not mean zero added latency between regions, and how would you diagnose unexpectedly high cross-region latency inside one VPC?
drills.a: Global VPC removes the CONFIGURATION burden of cross-region reachability (no peering/transit needed), but physical distance and Google's backbone routing path still impose real latency -- 'global' describes the resource's scope, not a physics exemption. To diagnose unexpected latency: check whether the actual traffic path is going through an internal load balancer scoped to the wrong region, a route misconfiguration forcing a suboptimal path, or backend selection issues -- not assume the VPC-global property itself is broken, since it only guarantees reachability, not any particular latency bound.

drills.q: Explain when a regional load balancer is the correct choice over the global external Application Load Balancer, even for an internet-facing production service.
drills.a: Data-residency requirements mandating traffic stay within a specific jurisdiction's routing path; active-passive DR designs needing explicit manual/scripted control over which region serves traffic rather than automatic nearest-PoP routing; genuinely single-region user bases where global anycast's cost premium and Premium Tier networking requirement buy nothing; or a deliberate choice of Standard Tier (cheaper, internet-routed) networking over Premium Tier backbone routing. Cloud Armor still attaches to regional LBs, but the edge-absorption DDoS benefit tied to global anycast's PoP distribution is lost.
